summary: Congress-funded 1838 light in East Penobscot Bay: a Ball family of keepers, a 1917 assist, a 1959 automation and a 1963 fight over the keeper's house.

structures.note: Original tower 25 ft (7.6 m) per LighthouseFriends and caretakers; the archive gives 30 ft to the centre of the lantern.

access.note: Reached by boat. The U.S. Lighthouse Society's archive lists the station as not open to the public; LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the tower closed.

events.note: Congress allocates $5,000 for the light (3 March 1837)
Tower built, rubblestone; first lit by John Spear
Lit late September 1838 (LighthouseFriends gives 28 September)
Keeper's 1842 report describes leaks, ice inside the tower and rotten mortar
Caretakers say the original light was 'largely reconstructed' in 1857; LighthouseFriends does not mention a rebuilt tower. Disputed.
Wooden keeper's house replaces the stone one
Fourth-order Fresnel lens; the archive gives 1858, LighthouseFriends and the caretakers 1857
Fuel changes from whale oil or lard to kerosene
Oil house built; a flight of stairs built up the bluff
Boundary fence built around the reservation
Edward S. Farren takes charge after Howard T. Ball's death
Keeper Howard T. Ball dies early in 1913 after guiding a fishing vessel to safety in a storm
Keeper E. S. Farren assists the captain of a sloop stricken with heart disease (4 December 1917)
1,200-lb bell hung outside the wooden pyramidal tower
Coast Guard takes over the station's operation (sources differ on the mechanism)
Fresnel lens replaced by a 300 mm lens on battery and diesel power; flashing white every four seconds; fog bell turned off
Keeper's dwelling and other buildings burned by the Coast Guard, over islanders' opposition; lighthouse and bell tower kept
Fog bell broke loose during removal and fell into the water; later recovered by a local fisherman
Light transferred to Eagle Light Caretakers under the Maine Lights Program (the caretakers' date; LighthouseFriends gives no year)
Coast Guard attempts to discontinue the light; it remains an active aid
Multi-phase restoration with J.B. Leslie Company; phases dated 2017, 2018 and 2023 by LighthouseFriends; final phases on hold per the caretakers

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1838 for the tower and 1858 for the lens and first lighting in Wikidata's record. The caretakers and LighthouseFriends give 1838 for the first lighting by Spear and 1857 for the lens; the caretakers say the tower was 'largely reconstructed' in 1857, which LighthouseFriends does not mention. The story keeps the 1838 first lighting and reports the rebuilding question as open.
LighthouseFriends says rubblestone; the caretakers say granite block outside, brick inside, rubblestone between; the archive says granite rubblestone. The story gives all three.

resolved_conflicts.field: keeper name (Frank E. Bracey / Frank E. Bracey Jr.)
resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive lists Frank E. Bracey (1931-1945). The caretakers' history calls the last civilian keeper Frank E. Bracey Jr. LighthouseFriends describes a Frank E. Bracey, Jr. as the keeper's son. The sources do not settle which name belongs to the keeper; the story says so.

LighthouseFriends dates a 76-step stairway to 1894. The Board's 1895 report records a flight of stairs built up the bluff on the southeast side of the reservation. The caretakers describe a 76-step wooden stairway on the eastern side of the cliff, without a date. The sources do not say whether these are one structure; the story says so.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on the first tower and the 1857/1858 lens and rebuilding; the story says so. Name variants: the caretakers call the last civilian keeper Frank E. Bracey Jr.; LighthouseFriends calls Frank E. Bracey, Jr. the keeper's son; the archive lists Frank E. Bracey (1931-1945). The Commissioner's fiscal 1918 table (printed p. 48, scan p. 362) was checked on the page image: the row reads E. L. Farren, keeper, Eagle Island Light Station, with the act 'Rendered assistance to sick captain of sloop'. The OCR gives 'E. L. Fan-en'. The initials differ from the Bulletin's E. S. Farren and from the fiscal 1919 table (printed p. 59, clean OCR, E. S. Farren). The row was matched to the Bulletin's 4 December 1917 entry by station, keeper and act. The 1896 boundary-fence line is OCR'd with errors and is quoted as printed. The 1895 stairway (southeast side), LighthouseFriends' 1894 76-step stairway and the caretakers' 76-step stairway on the eastern side are not confirmed as one structure; the story says so. Not used: the Wikipedia article (lead only) which says the first tower was torn down; no primary source found for that. The 1913 newspaper search for Howard T. Ball did not return a verified page. Eagle Island in Casco Bay (Peary's home) is a different island and was not used. LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site; only facts and short quotations were used. The archive's 1998 transfer date mentioned in a search snippet was not confirmed on the archive page, so 1996 (caretakers) is used. Roster lines carry the archive's person slugs as printed by roster.py. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Banks sentence now cites LighthouseFriends only (the archive does not carry the statement); the 1945 takeover cites both sources and the sentence on how it happened was reworded to what each source says.
